'''Lynn Justine Rothschild''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FLS}} (born May 11, 1957) is an [[evolutionary biology|evolutionary biologist]], [[astrobiologist]] and [[Synthetic biology|synthetic biologist]] at NASA's [[Ames Research Center]],<ref>[https://www.sciencefriday.com/articles/to-survive-on-mars-byo-bacteria/ "To Survive on Mars, BYO Bacteria"] ''Science Friday''. Retrieved 2017-03-14.</ref><ref>[http://astrobiology.nasa.gov/directory/profile/845/lynn/ Lynn Rothschild.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110909083427/http://astrobiology.nasa.gov/directory/profile/845/lynn/ |date=2011-09-09 }} NASA 2011. Retrieved 14 September 2011.</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Lynn J. Rothschild - NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/people/lynn-j-rothschild/ |access-date=2024-08-17 |language=en-US}}</ref> and is an [[adjunct professor]] at [[Brown University]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Rothschild, Lynn |url=https://vivo.brown.edu/display/lr3 |access-date=2024-08-17 |website=vivo.brown.edu}}</ref> She is an adjunct professor at [[Stanford University]], where she teaches [http://www.stanford.edu/group/astrobiology/cgi-bin/ Astrobiology and Space Exploration]. At Ames, her research has focused on how life, particularly microbes, has evolved in the context of the physical environment, both on Earth and potentially beyond our planet's boundaries. Her research also explores the use of synthetic biology as an enabling tool for space travel.<ref name=":0" /> Since 2007, she has studied the effect of [[UV radiation]] on DNA synthesis, carbon metabolism and mutation/DNA repair in the [[Great Rift Valley, Kenya|Rift Valley]] of Kenya and the Bolivian Andes, and also in high altitude experiments atop [[Mount Everest]], in balloon payloads with [[BioLaunch]]. She was the principal investigator of the first free-flyer synthetic biology payload which flew on the DLR [[EuCROPIS]] mission. In 2024, she received a Phase III NIAC grant to explore the use of [[Fungus|fungi]] for constructing habitats on the [[Moon]] or [[Mars]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=NASA Advances Research to Grow Habitats in Space from Fungi - NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-advances-research-to-grow-habitats-in-space-from-fungi/ |access-date=2024-08-17 |language=en-US}}</ref>

Rothschild graduated from [[Yale University]] in 1978 and earned a Ph.D. from [[Brown University]] in 1985.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> In addition to leading her research group at Ames, she serves as the Bio and Bio-Inspired Technologies, Research and Technology Lead for [[NASA]] Headquarters Space Technology Mission Directorate.<ref name=":0" /> Rothschild founded the [https://www.agu.org/abscicon Astrobiology Science Conferences] and the ''[[International Journal of Astrobiology]]''.<ref name=":0" /> From 2011-2019, she served a faculty Advisor for the Stanford-Brown [[iGEM]] teams, which utilized synthetic biology to advance NASA's mission objectives, including BioWires and a biodegradable drone.<ref name=":0" />

== Early life and education ==
Lynn Rothschild was born on May 11, 1957, in [[New York City]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |date=2020-04-29 |title=Interview with Lynn Rothschild from Planetary Systems Branch - NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/general/interview-with-lynn-rothschild-from-planetary-systems-branch/ |access-date=2024-08-17 |language=en-US}}</ref> She lived in [[Riverdale, Bronx|Riverdale]] until the age of eight, after which her family moved to [[Greenwich, Connecticut]].<ref name=":2" /> Rothschild attributes her initial interest in science to an experience in the third grade when she first looked through a microscope. Recalling this moment in an interview, she stated, "The third day I saw an amoeba, and that was it–I was hooked! So I’ve wanted to be a protozoologist literally since I was eight years old."<ref name=":2" />

Rothschild was an undergraduate student at [[Yale University]] in [[New Haven, Connecticut]], where she studied biology.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> During her time at Yale, she was mentored by prominent figures in the fields of phylogeny and organismal biology, including [[G. Evelyn Hutchinson]], [[John Ostrom]], and Willard Harman.<ref name=":2" /> In her junior year, she met John Preer Jr., a ciliate geneticist from [[Indiana University]] who was on sabbatical at Yale.<ref name=":2" /> This encounter led Rothschild to pursue a Master's degree in [[Zoology]] at Indiana University, which she completed in 1981 under the supervision of [[Tracy Sonneborn]], a renowned [[Protozoa|protozoan]] geneticist.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /> Following Sonneborn's death, Rothschild transferred to [[Brown University]] to continue her graduate studies.<ref name=":2" /> 

At Brown, Rothschild joined the algal research lab of [[Annette W. Coleman]], where she focused on chloroplast evolution and the isolation of [[RuBisCO]].<ref name=":2" /> She earned her Ph.D. in 1985 with a dissertation titled "Assessment of evolutionary relationships among protistan phyla and a blue-green prokaryote by comparison of the enzyme ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase."<ref name=":0" /> Rothschild then completed a postdoctoral fellowship at Brown in the laboratory of [[Susan Gerbi]], where she conducted research on [[yeast]] and the evolution of [[ribosomal DNA]].<ref name=":2" />

== NASA career and research ==
After completing her postdoctoral fellowship at Brown University, Rothschild was a National Research Council Postdoctoral Fellow at [[Ames Research Center|NASA Ames Research Center]] from 1987 to 1990.<ref name=":0" />  During this period, she conducted fieldwork and investigated the evolution of microbial mats and carbon fixation.<ref name=":2" /> in 1997, Rothschild became a Research Scientist at NASA Ames and then became a Senior Scientist in the Space Sciences Branch in 2015.<ref name=":1" /> 

=== Synthetic biology research and iGEM ===
Rothschild led the Synthetic Biology Program at NASA Ames from 2010 to 2011 and again from 2013 to 2015.<ref name=":1" /> She is also a member of the Build-a-Cell steering group, with interest in designing genomes and cells.<ref>{{Cite web |title=101 |url=https://www.buildacell.org/101 |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=Build-a-Cell |language=en-US}}</ref>  In 2024, Rothschild was awarded a Phase III NIAC grant for her Mycotecture Off Planet project.<ref name=":3" /> This initiative focuses on leveraging [[Fungus|fungi]] to create habitats for [[Astronaut|astronauts]] on long duration missions to the Moon and Mars.<ref name=":3" /> In addition to her work with mycotecture, Rothschild is also exploring the application of spore-forming [[bacteria]] to produce on demand medicine for astronauts.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-04-07 |title=An Astropharmacy - NASA |url=https://www.nasa.gov/general/an-astropharmacy/ |access-date=2024-08-21 |language=en-US}}</ref>

Rothschild served as a faculty advisor for several Brown-Stanford teams competing in the international synthetic biology competition, [[International Genetically Engineered Machine|iGEM]].<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=iGEM |url=https://igem.org |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=igem.org |language=en}}</ref>  Notable projects she superviesed include:

* Synthetic biology for Mars Exploration (2011)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Team:Brown-Stanford/PowerCell/Introduction - 2011.igem.org |url=https://2011.igem.org/Team:Brown-Stanford/PowerCell/Introduction |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=2011.igem.org}}</ref>
* Synthetic biology for astrobiology, including biomining (2012)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Team:Stanford-Brown - 2012.igem.org |url=https://2012.igem.org/Team:Stanford-Brown |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=2012.igem.org}}</ref>
* Synthetic biocommunication (2013)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Team:Stanford-Brown/Projects/EuCROPIS - 2013.igem.org |url=https://2013.igem.org/Team:Stanford-Brown/Projects/EuCROPIS |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=2013.igem.org}}</ref>
* Towards a Biodegradable UAS (2014), advised for the Stanford-Brown-Spelman iGEM team<ref>{{Cite web |title=Team:StanfordBrownSpelman - 2014.igem.org |url=https://2014.igem.org/Team:StanfordBrownSpelman#SBS%20iGEM |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=2014.igem.org}}</ref>
* BiOrigami (2015)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Team:Stanford-Brown - 2015.igem.org |url=https://2015.igem.org/Team:Stanford-Brown |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=2015.igem.org}}</ref>
* BioBalloon (2016)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Team:Stanford-Brown - 2016.igem.org |url=https://2016.igem.org/Team:Stanford-Brown |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=2016.igem.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=As competition concludes, 'bio balloon' team has reached great heights {{!}} Brown University |url=https://www.brown.edu/news/2016-10-26/igem |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=www.brown.edu |language=en}}</ref>
* Mars: getting there and staying there (2017)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Team:Stanford-Brown - 2017.igem.org |url=https://2017.igem.org/Team:Stanford-Brown |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=2017.igem.org}}</ref>
* Myco for Mars (2018), advised for the Stanford-Brown-RISD iGEM team<ref>{{Cite web |title=Team:Stanford-Brown-RISD - 2018.igem.org |url=https://2018.igem.org/Team:Stanford-Brown-RISD |access-date=2024-08-21 |website=2018.igem.org}}</ref>

=== Ultraviolet radiation research ===
Rothschild has explored the impact of ultraviolet (UV) radiation on life, both on Earth and potentially on other planetary bodies.<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last=Rothschild |first=L. J. |date=1999 |title=The influence of UV radiation on protistan evolution |journal=The Journal of Eukaryotic Microbiology |volume=46 |issue=5 |pages=548–555 |doi=10.1111/j.1550-7408.1999.tb06074.x |issn=1066-5234 |pmid=11536924}}</ref><ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last1=Rothschild |first1=L. J. |last2=Cockell |first2=C. S. |date=1999-12-06 |title=Radiation: microbial evolution, ecology, and relevance to mars missions |journal=Mutation Research |volume=430 |issue=2 |pages=281–291 |doi=10.1016/s0027-5107(99)00140-2 |issn=0027-5107 |pmid=10631343}}</ref> She suggests that [[UV radiation]] may have been critical in the evolution of the first [[Eukaryote|eukaryotic cells]] and in the origin of [[sexual reproduction]].<ref name=":7" /> In addition, Rothschild has written about how understanding the impact of UV radiation on microbes on Earth is important for future missions to Mars.<ref name=":8" /> 

=== Microbial Mats and Insights in Evolutionary Biology and Astrobiology ===
Rothschild has conducted research on [[microbial mat]]s, using them as models for early Earth and Martian ecosystems.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Rothschild |first1=Lynn J. |last2=Mancinelli |first2=Rocco L. |date=June 1990 |title=Model of carbon fixation in microbial mats from 3,500 Myr ago to the present |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/345710a0 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=345 |issue=6277 |pages=710–712 |doi=10.1038/345710a0 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last=Rothschild |first=L. J |date=1995-03-01 |title=A "cryptic" microbial mat: A new model ecosystem for extant life on Mars |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S027311779980088X |journal=Advances in Space Research |volume=15 |issue=3 |pages=223–228 |doi=10.1016/S0273-1177(99)80088-X |issn=0273-1177|url-access=subscription }}</ref> One of her studies focused on carbon fixation in microbial mats located in [[evaporation pond]]s of the [[Ojo de Liebre Lagoon]] in [[Baja California, Mexico]].<ref name=":5" /> These mats were selected as analogs for [[stromatolite]] fossils during the [[Proterozoic]] period due to their similar level of dissolved inorganic carbon to those predicted in ancient ocean models.<ref name=":5" /> The findings from this study led to the hypothesis that the decline of stromatolites might have been due to a decline in available carbon dioxide.<ref name=":5" /> 

In addition to her work on early Earth analogs, Rothschild has explored carbon fixation in near-surface microbial communities on Earth as model ecosystems for potential extant life on Mars.<ref name=":6" /> Her research includes studies in the supertidal of Laguna Ojo de Liebre and small geysers in [[Yellowstone National Park]].<ref name=":6" /> At Yellowstone, Rothschild investigated microbial mats living in acidic environments beneath gravel.<ref name=":6" /> Drawing on the characteristics of these two Earth ecosystems, Rothschild concluded that “it is not unreasonable to speculate that a near-surface community, such as the Baja and Yellowstone sites described here, might be found on Mars.”<ref name=":6" />

== Awards and honors ==
Lynn Rothschild has received numerous accolades throughout her career. She has been a NASA Innovative Advanced Concepts (NIAC) fellow five times.<ref name=":1" /> In 2015, she was awarded the Horace Mann Medal by the Brown University Graduate School, which recognized her as "a pioneer in Astrobiology" and acknowledged her influential role in space and life science education.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Horace Mann Medal Winners {{!}} Graduate School {{!}} Brown University |url=https://graduateschool.brown.edu/about/academic-events-honors/awards/horace-mann-medal/horace-mann-medal-winners |access-date=2024-08-27 |website=graduateschool.brown.edu |language=en}}</ref> The same year she also received the [[American Humanist Association]]'s Isaac Asimov Science Award.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-08-27 |title=Annual Humanist Awardees |url=https://americanhumanist.org/awardees/ |access-date=2024-08-27 |website=American Humanist Association |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Humanist |first=The |date=2015-10-20 |title=Battlestar Galapagos: Where Are We Going, Where Have We Been, and Are We Alone? |url=https://thehumanist.com/magazine/november-december-2015/features/battlestar-galapagos-where-are-we-going-where-havewe-been-and-are-we-alone |access-date=2024-08-27 |website=TheHumanist.com |language=en-US}}</ref> 

Rothschild has been elected as a fellow to several organizations, including the [[Linnean Society of London]], the [[California Academy of Sciences]] and the Explorer's Club.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":4" /> Additionally, she served as the president of the Society of Protozoologists from 2002 to 2003.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />
